content: Thiamine, also referred to as vitamin B1 or aneurine hydrochloride, is a water-soluble compound that belongs to the B-vitamin family. Its chemical formula is C12H17N4OS, and it is characterized by a pyrimidine ring and a thiazole ring in its structure. Thiamine is colorless, soluble in water, and insoluble in alcohol. It is unstable when exposed to heat, leading to its decomposition. Thiamine was first identified in 1910 by Umetaro Suzuki in Japan during his research on rice bran's ability to cure beriberi. He initially named it aberic acid, later referred to as orizanin, but he did not determine its chemical structure or recognize it as an amine. In 1926, Jansen and Donath successfully crystallized the compound and named it aneurin, highlighting its antineuritic properties. The complete chemical composition and synthesis of thiamine were elucidated in 1935 by Robert R. Williams, who also coined the term thiamine. Thiamine exists in several natural phosphate derivatives, including thiamine monophosphate (ThMP), thiamine diphosphate (ThDP) or thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), thiamine triphosphate (ThTP), and adenosine thiamine triphosphate (AThTP), which was more recently discovered. Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), also known as thiamine diphosphate (ThDP), functions as a coenzyme for various enzymes involved in the metabolism of alpha-keto acids. In mammals, TPP is essential for enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, which are critical for carbohydrate metabolism. It also supports the activity of branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, 2-hydroxyphytanoyl-CoA lyase, and transketolase, the latter of which plays a role in the pentose phosphate pathway to produce NADPH and pentose sugars like ribose and deoxyribose. In other species, TPP is involved in enzymes such as pyruvate decarboxylase in yeast and additional bacterial enzymes. The synthesis of TPP requires the enzyme thiamine pyrophosphokinase, along with free thiamine, magnesium, and adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Thiamine triphosphate (ThTP) was historically thought to be a neuroactive form of thiamine. However, recent findings indicate that ThTP is present in bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals, suggesting a broader cellular role. In Escherichia coli (E. coli), ThTP appears to play a role in the cellular response to amino acid starvation. Adenosine thiamine triphosphate (AThTP), or thiaminylated adenosine triphosphate, is a recently identified derivative of thiamine. It accumulates in E. coli during carbon starvation and can constitute up to 20% of the total thiamine content in these bacteria. Smaller amounts of AThTP have also been detected in yeast, plant roots, and animal tissues. Thiamine is vital for the metabolism of carbohydrates and fats, enabling the body to produce energy. It is essential for normal growth and development and supports the proper functioning of the heart, nervous system, and digestive system. As a water-soluble vitamin, thiamine cannot be stored in the body and must be obtained regularly through dietary sources. Once absorbed, it is concentrated in muscle tissue. Good dietary sources of thiamine include green peas, spinach, liver, beef, pork, navy beans, nuts, pinto beans, bananas, soybeans, goji berries, whole grains, breads, yeast, the aleurone layer of unpolished rice, and legumes. Each of these foods contains at least 0.1 mg of thiamine per 28–100 grams. A deficiency in thiamine can lead to severe health issues, including neurodegeneration, muscle wasting, and even death. Causes of deficiency include malnutrition, chronic alcoholism, and diets high in thiaminase-rich foods (e.g., raw freshwater fish, raw shellfish, ferns) or foods containing anti-thiamine factors (e.g., tea, coffee, betel nuts). Well-known conditions associated with thiamine deficiency include Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi, both of which are commonly observed in individuals with chronic alcoholism. Additionally, thiamine deficiency is thought to be prevalent in many individuals with diabetes, potentially contributing to complications associated with the disease. Thiamine deficiency can be diagnosed by measuring the activity of the enzyme transketolase in erythrocytes. Alternatively, thiamine levels can be assessed directly in whole blood by converting thiamine into a fluorescent thiochrome derivative. However, some cases of deficiency may not be detected using these methods. Genetic disorders affecting thiamine transport are rare but significant. Thiamine-Responsive Megaloblastic Anemia (TRMA) is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the SLC19A2 gene, which encodes a high-affinity thiamine transporter. TRMA is characterized by megaloblastic anemia, diabetes mellitus, and sensorineural deafness. Interestingly, systemic thiamine deficiency is not observed in TRMA patients, suggesting redundancy in the thiamine transport system. This has led to the identification of a second high-affinity thiamine transporter, SLC19A3. The recommended daily allowance (RDA) for thiamine is approximately 1.4 mg in most countries. However, studies have suggested that higher doses, such as 50 mg daily, may enhance mental acuity. Additionally, thiamine has been investigated as a potential insect repellent. Doses of 25–50 mg taken three times daily are thought to reduce mosquito bites by producing a skin odor that is imperceptible to humans but repellent to female mosquitoes. This effect requires at least two weeks of supplementation to fully saturate the skin. While anecdotal evidence supports the efficacy of thiamine-based repellents, clinical trials are lacking. A 2002 pilot study explored the use of thiamine tetrahydrofurfuryl disulfide (TTFD) in children with autism spectrum disorder. Administered rectally, TTFD appeared to produce beneficial effects in eight out of ten participants. However, this study has not been replicated, and a subsequent 2006 review by the same author did not address thiamine's potential role in autism.
